newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Mixed day for markets as funds leave coffee.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mixed day for markets as funds leave coffee.

text.p: Coffee prices slumped on Tuesday as speculative investment funds decided the market's rally had run its course and they would collect profits elsewhere.
Elsewhere copper values gyrated and wheat and corn prices
firmed on what
traders here described as a "weather market" in Chicago.
The result for coffee was a drop in London coffee futures
prices for robusta beans by around 10 percent over the day.
London's benchmark contract for the September delivery sank to a day's low of $1,565 per tonne, the lowest level seen since mid-April. It closed a steep $150 down at $1,585.
The bale-out followed a five-month rally that peaked in May when prices touched 20-month highs of $2,700.

A volatile mix of low stocks, tight Latin American supply and worries that leading producer Brazil might have another damaging frost had lured a wave of speculative money to the coffee futures market.
But Tuesday's reversal took prices back to nearly half what they were on May 29.
"It's all fund selling," said one trader. "They were long in the market, now it's not clear whether they are short of it."
No strong signs have yet emerged of the market turning, but it might rebound slightly in a technical correction to the heavy sell-off, analysts said.
Traders said the decline was purely chart-driven as London took little heed of a relatively calm New York futures market for premium arabica coffee.

Coffee consumption traditionally dips during the northern hemisphere summer, and this year the market also faces a consumer reaction to the sharp retail price increases that followed the earlier futures rally from January lows of around $1,200.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) copper market slid below $2,300 a tonne in whipsaw trading, dealers said.
Copper's choppy behaviour was reflected throughout the base metals complex, with most LME metals ending the afternoon kerb in the minus column.
Flagship three months copper came off an early high of $2,337 to finish just above the day's lows at $2,278, compared to Monday's kerb close of $2,315.
"They're all looking sorrowful, taking the lead from copper. Once copper turned lower there was no stopping the other metals," a trader said.

Gold prices were fairly steady just above the near 12-year lows hit last week but bullion dealers said they were disappointed there was not more of a reaction to a report that a union official expected Russia's production this year to be only 90 tonnes compared with an estimated 130 tonnes last year.
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) soft red winter wheat futures were boasted by a rally in corn futures, traders said.
Corn's firmness came from forecasts for a continuation of hot, dry weather in the U.S. Midwest which could interfere with that crop's key pollination stage of development.
Dry weather in portions of Australia's wheat growing region also led to the advances but fund buying was pitted against commercial selling, the traders said.
